_comment: Who a Layers note may cite. Shubhanshu's rule (2026-10-11): cite Bible-believing people who fully believe the Bible and theologians who love God, not people who liberalize the Bible to mean something else. A note goes live once it cites at least one source from "cite" (checked by crates/atlas-cli/src/layers.rs); a note with none stays hidden until a person reviews its passage.

cite: one entry per work a note may cite. id: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, used in a note's cites. role: "interpreter" for a commentary or teacher, "reference" for a translation, word book or dictionary; a wordplay, allusion, pattern, irony or fulfillment note needs at least one interpreter. name: as the app shows it ("Keil and Delitzsch"). title, by, when: what the work is. biblehub: the work's code on biblehub.com/commentaries, so a cite "on" a verse links to that chapter there. url: a page to read the work when it has no Bible Hub code. why: one plain sentence on why it passes the rule. not_on: books whose volume of a many-handed set is not cited, with the reason in why.

avoid: works and writers a note may not cite or name, because they read the Bible along higher-critical lines, because we could not confirm they hold the whole Bible true, or because they write outside the Christian faith. Shubhanshu chose Christian writers only (2026-10-11): Catholic and Orthodox writers who uphold Scripture may be cited; rabbis' commentaries and Jewish scholars may not. match: words that name it, found where a word starts; the build stops on any of them in a note's text or evidence or a passage's source.

Ancient writings (the Septuagint, Targums, Mishnah, Talmud, Midrash, Josephus, Philo, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Apocrypha) may be named in evidence as witnesses to what people read or believed, but they are not interpreters and never count as a note's citation.

cite.title: Berean Standard Bible and its footnotes
cite.why: Translated by Bible-believing scholars; its footnotes mark where the New Testament quotes the Old.

cite.name: Matthew Henry
cite.title: Commentary on the Whole Bible
cite.why: A pastor's commentary that takes every word of Scripture as God's word.

cite.name: Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary
cite.title: Concise Commentary on the Whole Bible
cite.why: The short form of Matthew Henry's commentary.

cite.name: John Gill
cite.title: Exposition of the Old and New Testaments
cite.why: A verse-by-verse exposition that holds Scripture to be inspired and without error, often quoting old Jewish writings.

cite.name: Albert Barnes
cite.title: Notes on the Bible
cite.why: Notes written to help ordinary readers believe and understand the whole Bible.

cite.name: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown
cite.title: Commentary, Critical and Explanatory, on the Whole Bible
cite.by: Robert Jamieson, A. R. Fausset and David Brown
cite.why: A conservative commentary that defends the Bible's inspiration and its prophecies of Christ.

cite.name: Keil and Delitzsch
cite.title: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament
cite.by: Carl Friedrich Keil and Franz Delitzsch, Lutheran scholars
cite.why: A close reading of the Hebrew that defends the Old Testament against the critics of its day.

cite.name: the Pulpit Commentary
cite.title: The Pulpit Commentary
cite.by: Edited by H. D. M. Spence and Joseph S. Exell
cite.why: Written by believing pastors and scholars for preaching the whole Bible, except the volume on Jeremiah and Lamentations, by the higher critic T. K. Cheyne, which is not cited.

cite.name: Ellicott's Commentary
cite.title: Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers
cite.by: Edited by Charles John Ellicott, Bishop of Gloucester
cite.why: A believing commentary edited by a bishop who defended the Bible's inspiration.

cite.name: Joseph Benson
cite.title: Commentary on the Old and New Testaments
cite.why: A Methodist preacher's commentary that holds the whole Bible as God's word.

cite.name: Matthew Poole
cite.title: Annotations upon the Holy Bible
cite.why: A Puritan commentary that reads Scripture as God's word throughout.

cite.name: John Calvin
cite.title: Commentaries
cite.why: The Reformer's commentaries, which take Scripture as the final word of God.

cite.name: Adam Clarke
cite.title: Commentary on the Bible
cite.why: A Methodist scholar's commentary that holds the Bible as God's word.

cite.name: John Wesley
cite.title: Explanatory Notes upon the Old and New Testaments
cite.why: Brief notes by the founder of Methodism, who held Scripture to be without error.

cite.name: the Geneva Bible notes
cite.title: Geneva Study Bible notes
cite.why: The Reformation-era study notes that the Puritans read.

cite.name: Bengel
cite.title: Gnomon of the New Testament
cite.why: A devout scholar's notes on the Greek, written to honour every word of Scripture.

cite.name: Alexander Maclaren
cite.title: Expositions of Holy Scripture
cite.why: Sermons on the text by a Baptist preacher who held the Bible as God's word.

cite.name: Spurgeon
cite.title: The Treasury of David
cite.why: Spurgeon's work on the Psalms; he defended the Bible's full inspiration.

cite.name: John Chrysostom
cite.title: Homilies
cite.why: A church father who preached Scripture as God's word.

cite.title: Writings of the early church
cite.by: Christian teachers of the first centuries, such as Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, Augustine and Jerome

cite.name: Alfred Edersheim

cite.name: the NET Bible notes

cite.name: the Reformation Study Bible

cite.name: Abbott-Smith

avoid.name: the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges
avoid.why: Several volumes, such as S. R. Driver's, John Skinner's and A. B. Davidson's, read the Old Testament along higher-critical lines.

avoid.name: the Expositor's Greek Testament

avoid.name: the Expositor's Bible
avoid.why: Volumes such as George Adam Smith's on Isaiah and Marcus Dods's on Genesis follow higher-critical views.

avoid.name: Meyer's Critical and Exegetical Commentary

avoid.name: the International Critical Commentary
avoid.why: Written mostly from the higher-critical view of the Bible.

avoid.name: Brown-Driver-Briggs (BDB)
avoid.why: Its editors S. R. Driver and C. A. Briggs led the higher criticism; Briggs was suspended from the Presbyterian ministry in 1893 over his view of Scripture.

avoid.name: Thayer's Greek lexicon
avoid.why: Joseph Henry Thayer was a Unitarian, who denied the Trinity.

avoid.name: Vincent's Word Studies
avoid.why: We could not confirm its writer holds the whole Bible true.

avoid.name: medieval and later rabbis' commentaries
